comparator.name: Medical Informatics
comparator.sourceNotes: The Dutch-taught bachelor has 60 EC each year. The third year combines 18 EC of open electives, 18 EC of taught courses and a 24 EC internship and thesis. The regulations specify progression and a competency portfolio that must pass before the internship and thesis.

components.name: Clinical Epidemiology and Biostatistics
components.note: Entry to year two requires 48 EC from year one under the binding study advice rules.

components.name: Exchange of Health Data and Knowledge
Strategic Information Management
components.note: The academic and professional competency portfolio is assessed during this course.

components.name: Artificial Intelligence
components.note: Entry to year three requires all 60 EC of year one and at least 48 EC from year two.

components.name: Free-Choice Electives
components.note: Choose one or more electives for 18 EC. Choices outside the preapproved list require Examination Board approval.

components.name: Bachelor’s Internship and Thesis
components.note: Pass the academic and professional competency portfolio before starting the internship and thesis. The regulations place both in the second semester of year three.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Three options cover health information systems and software, biomedical data and signals, and health behaviour and digital innovation. Software development is part of the closest option. The digital innovation option focuses on users, evidence and organisational change.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both use statistical models and study design. UCR focuses on health and behaviour experiments, while UvA pairs biostatistics with clinical epidemiology.
Both study population health, disease patterns and determinants. UvA connects these topics to its healthcare curriculum.
Both use programming to build working software. UvA applies it to healthcare applications.
Both study organising and retrieving data. UvA addresses how healthcare systems exchange information and knowledge.
Both use logic and formal reasoning. UvA applies these ideas to medical diagnosis.
Both study machine learning. UvA applies AI in the context of healthcare and clinical information.
Both analyse digital images. UCR uses general image-processing and computer-vision methods, while UvA covers medical imaging and signals.
Both develop software design and construction skills. UvA embeds software engineering in medical informatics.
Both develop ideas from user needs and consider how to implement them. UvA focuses on innovation in healthcare.
Both study organisational decisions about technology and change. UvA focuses on information management in healthcare.
